facts.statement: Mystriosuchus was first named by Eberhard Fraas in 1896.
facts.quote: It was first named by Eberhard Fraas in 1896

facts.statement: Mystriosuchus lived in Europe and Greenland during the Late Triassic (middle Norian).
facts.quote: Mystriosuchus (meaning "spoon-crocodile") is an extinct genus of phytosaur that lived in the Late Triassic (middle Norian) in Europe and Greenland.

facts.statement: A complete skeleton found in 1995 indicates that M. planirostris measured about 4 meters in length.
facts.quote: Mystriosuchus planirostris measured about 4 m, according to a complete skeleton which was found in 1995.

facts.statement: Its long jaws, similar to modern gharials, suggest a primarily fish-eating diet.
facts.quote: Cranial morphology is suggestive of a primarily fish eating diet, having long jaws like those of the modern gharials.

facts.statement: Microwear studies indicate a preference for softer invertebrates in addition to fish.
facts.quote: A study on phytosaur microwear shows a preference towards softer invertebrates.

facts.statement: M. planirostris has a plain snout lacking bony ornamentation or crests.
facts.quote: M. planirostris, as the name implies, has a rather "plain" snout, without osseous ornamentation or crests.

facts.statement: M. westphali features multiple bony crests along the upper jaw, especially at the base and tip of the snout.
facts.quote: M. westphali, on the other hand, has multiple bony crests along the upper jaw, most prominently at the base and tip of the snout.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest M. planirostris may have had soft tissue ornamentation, similar to keratinous crests known in other phytosaurs.
facts.quote: As keratinous crests are known in phytosaurs, it is possible that M. planirostris had soft tissue ornamentation.

facts.statement: The tail makes up 51% of the total body length, making it longer than the rest of the body combined.
facts.quote: The tail is longer than the rest of the body, being 51% of the total length of the taxon.

facts.statement: The inverted 'T' shape of chevrons at the tail end is unique to Mystriosuchus among phytosaurs but seen in sauropterygians and some crocodilians.
facts.quote: At the end of the tail the vertebrae become more slanted, and the chevrons form an inverted 'T' shape, which is not seen in other phytosaurs but in sauropterygians or some crocodilians.

facts.statement: Cladistic analysis later grouped Mystriosuchus with Pseudopalatinae instead of its former subfamily, Mystriosuchidae.
facts.quote: Mystriosuchus used to be placed in its own subfamily, Mystriosuchidae, but subsequent cladistic analysis grouped it with other members of Pseudopalatinae

facts.statement: While originally thought to be freshwater, some specimens from Northern Italy indicate a completely marine lifestyle.
facts.quote: Originally considered to be a freshwater genus, a recent specimen from Northern Italy has shown that some Mystriosuchus specimens lived a completely marine life.

facts.statement: Mystriosuchus is classified within the subfamily Pseudopalatinae.
The genus authority for Mystriosuchus is Fraas, 1896.
The genus includes two species: M. westphali and the type species M. planirostris.
facts.quote: Fue nombrado originalmente por Eberhard Fraas en 1896, e incluye a dos especies: M. westphali y la especie tipo, M. planirostris.

facts.statement: Christian Kammerer and colleagues synonymized Pseudopalatinae with Mystriosuchini because the latter has priority.
facts.quote: En su artículo sobre Parasuchus, Christian Kammerer y colaboradores señalaron que Mystriosuchini tenía prioridad sobre Pseudopalatinae, por lo cual sinonimizaron a Pseudopalatinae con Mystriosuchini.

facts.statement: Mystriosuchus belongs to the parent group Mystriosuchini.
Mystriosuchus lived from the Norian to the Hettangian, between 227.3 and 199.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Norian to Hettangian (227.3 to 199.5 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Shorter, paddle-like limbs suggest Mystriosuchus was more adapted to aquatic life than other known phytosaurs.
rejected.quote: The postcranial anatomy of the skeleton suggests that Mystriosuchus was more adapted to aquatic life than other known phytosaurs, possessing shorter and more paddle-like limbs
